conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’ll be guiding you through a short screening today. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a way to see how your emotional health is doing in these first weeks and months postpartum.

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are just 10 questions, each asking about the past seven days. You can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it one question at a time. Ready to begin?

In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly? Not very often… maybe once or twice when my partner made a silly face at the baby, but even then the laugh felt kind of forced and faded fast. Most of the time nothing feels funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I can’t remember the last time I laughed without forcing it. Even when I try to watch something funny on my phone, it just feels flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with friends, a walk to the park—but lately it’s like… why bother? I still go, because I know I should, but the happy buzz I used to feel is gone. Maybe once this week I thought, “This might be nice,” but it fizzled before I even left the house.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby spits up a lot, I immediately think it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing or didn’t burp him long enough. When he wouldn’t settle last night, I kept replaying everything I did—maybe I held him too much, maybe I didn’t hold him enough. I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilty voice keeps saying I should be doing better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s stopped breathing—even though I can see his chest moving. I check the monitor a dozen times an hour. Sometimes the worry just loops: is the room too cold, too hot, is that sniffle RSV, am I missing something? There’s no real reason, but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times this week. It hits suddenly—like yesterday while folding laundry my chest got tight, heart pounding, and I had to sit down because I was sure something awful was about to happen. I couldn’t tell you what, just this wave of dread. It passed after a few minutes, but it keeps popping up out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. There are moments when I look at the sink full of bottles and the pile of laundry and it feels like I’m drowning—like I’ll never catch up. I get through it, but it’s exhausting, and by evening I’m snapping at my partner over nothing because I’m so overwhelmed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A couple of nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep even though the baby was down. My mind just kept circling—what if I’m doing everything wrong, what if he gets sick, what if I never feel like myself again? I’d lie there for an hour or more, and when I did drift off I’d jolt awake with my heart racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… pretty much every day. It’s like this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears coming for no real reason. I’m not crying all day, but that sad, heavy feeling is there most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week it boiled over. Yesterday I locked the bathroom door, turned on the faucet so no one would hear, and just sobbed into a towel because I couldn’t get the baby to nap. The other time was after a doctor’s appointment—everyone said I looked “great,” but inside I felt broken, and the tears started the second I got back to the car.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times… nothing planned, just these quick flashes—like when I’m rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and I’m so tired I think, “What if I just didn’t wake up tomorrow?” It scares me, and I push it away, but yeah, the thought’s popped in.

You've shared that since your baby arrived most days feel heavy and gray. The things that used to bring you joy-laughing at a show, meeting a friend-now feel flat or pointless, and you often feel overwhelmed by everyday tasks like bottles and laundry. You described sudden waves of panic, constant worry about your baby's safety, and hours spent checking the monitor, yet you still blame yourself whenever anything goes wrong. Even when your little one is sleeping, your mind races so much that sleep is hard to find, and you've had a few tearful moments alone in the bathroom because the pressure feels so big. You also mentioned fleeting thoughts of not waking up, which you quickly push away but which frighten you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh naturally and finds humor flat, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Loss of anticipatory joy, "happy buzz gone," only fleeting interest that "fizzled" maps to "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily self-blame over normal infant behaviors, persistent guilt, and cognitive distortion equating baby's discomfort with personal failure, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, irrational worry occurring 'pretty much all the time' with physical symptoms and compulsive checking, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses multiple sudden panic episodes this week that are intense, unexpected, and without clear trigger—matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, feeling 'drowning' and 'exhausting,' fitting 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>She describes multiple nights of trouble falling and staying asleep explicitly linked to anxious/unhappy thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness, described as a constant "gray cloud" with frequent unexplained tears, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes driven by distress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring passive suicidal thoughts ('quick flashes...what if I just didn't wake up'), aligning with 'Sometimes</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The patient meets core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day (<sym>gray cloud</sym>), markedly diminished interest (<sym>nothing feels funny</sym>), excessive inappropriate guilt (<sym>should be doing better</sym>), fatigue (<sym>exhausting</sym>), insomnia (<sym>mind keeps circling</sym>), and recurrent thoughts of death (<sym>what if I just didn't wake up</sym>). <sym>Anxiety symptoms</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym> are also prominent, consistent with comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or go to nearest ED if thoughts of not waking up return or intensify
3. Ask partner or trusted adult to stay with you until professional help is in place
4. Inquire about starting evidence-based treatment options such as <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress
6. Reach out to local <med>postpartum support group</med> or <med>PMAD warmline</med> for peer support
7. Practice small self-care steps: 15-minute outdoor walk, accepting help with housework, and resting when baby rests
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 1 yr (infant referenced)

A. Positive screening indicators  
- Depressed mood & marked anhedonia (Q1, 2, 8) – present daily  
- Frequent crying spells, tearfulness without precipitant (Q9)  
- Excessive/unwarranted guilt, self-blame re infant care (Q3)  
- Persistent anxiety, panic attacks, intrusive fears of infant harm (Q4, 5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, inability to cope with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (Q7)  

B. Safety-related endorsement  
- Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I just didn’t wake up”) reported twice; no plan or intent stated (Q10)

C. Summary  
Responses meet threshold for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; passive SI present. Immediate safety assessment and follow-up evaluation recommended to determine need for formal diagnosis, intervention, and supports.
